Tick-Borne Illness

treat suspected rickettsiosis before confirming it · a rash from the extremities inward · the platelet, sodium and liver triad · no rash: ehrlichiosis · an expanding ring: LymeWhere did the rash start, and what did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do?

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Fever and headache for days, then a rash that starts on the wrists and ankles and moves to the trunk, palms and soles, with low platelets, low sodium and raised liver enzymes in spring or summer: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF).
  • Start doxycycline on suspicion, in children of any age and in pregnancy; paired serology confirms it weeks later, and a negative early result changes nothing.
  • The same tick season, usually with no rash and a low white count: ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis, also treated with doxycycline. A single expanding ring at a bite: Lyme disease, a diagnosis made on sight.
What it is

Infections passed by tick bite. The board anchor is RMSF, a rickettsial small-vessel vasculitis that kills when treatment waits for proof.

Bug

RMSF: Rickettsia rickettsii, a gram-negative obligate intracellular bacterium that takes the Gram stain poorly and lives in vascular endothelium.

Ehrlichiosis: Ehrlichia chaffeensis in monocytes. Anaplasmosis: Anaplasma phagocytophilum in granulocytes (MEGA: monocytes ehrlichiosis, granulocytes anaplasmosis).

Lyme disease: the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi.

Babesiosis: Babesia, a protozoan that lives inside red cells.

Spread

RMSF: Dermacentor ticks, spring and summer, most often the South Atlantic and southeastern states despite the name; only 55 to 60% recall a bite.

Lyme, anaplasmosis and babesiosis: one vector, the Ixodes tick, in the Northeast and upper Midwest, so one bite can carry two infections.

Ehrlichiosis: the lone star tick, in the southeastern and south-central states.

Chain

Tick bite

R. rickettsii enters and multiplies in vascular endothelium

small-vessel vasculitis with leaky capillaries

rash, platelets used up in injured vessels, low sodium, liver injury

untreated, it may progress to encephalitis, hypotension, circulatory failure and death

Insights

The rash is late: most patients have one only by the sixth day of fever, so the first visit often shows fever and headache alone.

Serology lags the illness: titers are often negative in the first week, so the test that confirms RMSF cannot decide when to treat it.

Day 0tick bite, often unnoticed
2 to 14 daysfever, severe headache, muscle aches In practice: the MSD (Merck Sharp and Dohme) Manual gives an incubation of 3 to 12 days; the NBME explanation uses 2 to 14.
By the sixth day of fevera rash in most, typically wrists and ankles first, then inward
About 5 to 6 days into the rashthe spots turn petechial
2 to 10 weeksconvalescent titer: a fourfold rise confirms it
2Urgent risks
Urgent findings
FindingAction
Confusion, seizures or coma with fever and rashEncephalitis: doxycycline now; lumbar puncture when the central nervous system is involved.
Hypotension with a fast pulseVascular collapse under way: doxycycline with fluid and organ support.
Afebrile, rapidly ascending flaccid paralysis with normal sensation and no rash after a hikeTick paralysis: search the whole skin for the tick and remove it before breathing fails.
3Differential
Fever and rash after outdoor exposure
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF)Days of fever and headache, then a rash from the wrists and ankles inward to the palms and soles; low platelets, low sodium, high transaminases.Doxycycline now; send serology but do not wait for it.
Ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosisSame tick setting and prodrome; usually no rash; low white count; morulae in monocytes or neutrophils.Send a blood smear and polymerase chain reaction (PCR); give doxycycline meanwhile.
Lyme diseaseA single expanding ring at the bite, often clearing in the center; later facial palsy, heart block or arthritis of a large joint such as the knee.Diagnose erythema migrans on sight and give doxycycline.
Fever 5 days or more with nonexudative conjunctivitis, a polymorphous rash, a node, red swollen hands and feet; platelets climb.Count the criteria; red eyes alone do not make it.
Hours, not days, from fever to petechiae and purpura, then shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation.Check the tempo: hours to purpura, against days of fever before an extremity rash.
Dengue feverTropical travel and Aedes mosquitoes; pain behind the eyes, severe bone and muscle pain; low white count and platelets.Obtain a travel history: dengue needs time in the tropics or subtropics.
Measles (rubeola)Cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, then a rash from the head down that spares the palms and soles.The rash direction and the missing prodrome exclude it here.
Roseola (exanthema subitum)Days of high fever in an infant, then a blanching rash on the neck and trunk as the fever breaks.Supportive care.
Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease)Slapped cheeks, then a lacy rash, in a school-age child who is otherwise well.Check for slapped cheeks: parvovirus B19 in a well child, not RMSF.
BabesiosisThe same Ixodes tick; fever with hemolytic anemia, dark urine and jaundice; worst without a spleen.Order a blood smear for Maltese cross tetrads; treat with atovaquone plus azithromycin.
Typhoid feverSalmonella Typhi in an endemic region; fever and chills with abdominal pain and diarrhea.Send blood cultures.
Immune thrombocytopeniaLow platelets alone in a well, afebrile child; normal liver tests.Fever, rash and raised transaminases rule it out here.
Wilson diseaseKayser-Fleischer rings; liver and neuropsychiatric disease over months.Exclude it on tempo: a febrile rash over days, not disease over months.
AmebiasisBloody diarrhea with fever; a liver abscess on imaging.A normal CT and a rash exclude it; skip stool ova and parasites.
4Workup
Pause point
Febrile child, wrist and ankle petechiae, serology just sent Offered as wait for the titer or amoxicillin Can a test that turns positive weeks later decide when to treat? → Doxycycline now; the serology only confirms it later
Under age 8, suspected RMSF, parents fear tooth staining Offered as amoxicillin or chloramphenicol Does a short course stain teeth, and does any other drug work as well? → Doxycycline: short courses spare the teeth, and other drugs raise the risk of death
Summer tick bite, fever, a low white count, low platelets, no rash Offered as RMSF or babesiosis Is there a rash, and what sits inside the white cells? → Ehrlichiosis: morulae in monocytes; doxycycline as well

A missing tick bite lowers nothing: only 55 to 60% recall one.

5Diagnostic criteria
A clinical diagnosis: what makes RMSF the working diagnosis
ElementFinding
ExposureWooded or rural life in spring or summer; a recalled bite is not required
TempoDays of fever and severe headache before any rash
RashTypically wrists and ankles first, then trunk, palms and soles; blanching, then petechial
LabsLow platelets, low sodium, raised AST and ALT; prolonged prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times
RuleNo criteria set: the picture starts treatment (step 7); serology confirms it later (step 4)

The rash can be missing: fever, headache and malaise in the right setting start doxycycline, rash or not. A rash on the palms and soles has a short list: RMSF, coxsackievirus A, toxic shock syndrome and secondary syphilis (Rash Covering The Soles).

6Severity
What makes it severe
FindingMeaning
Confusion, delirium, seizures or comaEncephalitis
HypotensionSevere disease; circulatory failure may follow if untreated
Bleeding with long clotting timesCoagulopathy
Doxycycline started lateA worse outlook; early treatment improves it
Babesiosis with asplenia, older age or advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infectionSevere, sometimes fatal hemolysis
7Treatment
1

Rickettsial diseaseRMSF, ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis suspected

Doxycycline at every age and in pregnancy; continue until at least 3 days after the fever ends. Short courses (5 to 10 days) do not stain permanent teeth; the American Academy of Pediatrics accepts doxycycline under age 8 for courses up to 21 days.

2

Doxycycline not toleratedAllergy or intolerance

Desensitize and still give doxycycline: other antibiotics raise the risk of death. Chloramphenicol is a rare second line for RMSF only; it fails in ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis.

3

Early Lyme diseaseErythema migrans

Doxycycline, 10 days for a single lesion; in pregnancy, amoxicillin or cefuroxime; a child under 8 also takes doxycycline. In practice: amoxicillin or cefuroxime remains an accepted choice for a young child who cannot take doxycycline.

4

Lyme heart or nervesMeningitis, carditis or heart block

IV ceftriaxone; complete heart block may need a temporary pacemaker.

5

BabesiosisMild to moderate

Oral atovaquone plus azithromycin; the azithromycin goes IV when the disease is severe.

8Follow-up
After a tick bite and after the illness
WhenDo
Tick still attachedLift it out with fine forceps and steady traction on the head; never crush or squeeze it.
A bite with no symptoms in an RMSF areaNo antibiotic; come back for fever, headache or a rash.
Deer tick bite in a high-Lyme areaNo routine prophylaxis; one dose of doxycycline only in a narrow case. Guideline criteria: the tick was attached 36 hours or more, it came off within the last 72 hours, and 20% or more of local ticks carry Lyme; the dose is oral doxycycline 200 mg once.
Confirmed or probable RMSFReport it to public health: spotted fever rickettsioses are nationally notifiable.
Practice
  1. 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, headache and abdominal pain, now confused with a maculopapular rash on the arms and legs; platelets 46,000, AST 202, ALT 158; lives near woods; abdominal CT normal → Doxycycline → empiric treatment for Rocky Mountain spotted fever
  2. 10 yo with fever, an extremity rash, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis after wooded exposure; serology has been sent → Withholding antibiotics until serology returns → untreated disease progresses to vascular collapse
  3. 9 yo seen 10 days after a hike with a single expanding annular lesion showing central clearing and mild fatigue → Lyme disease → erythema migrans
  4. 4 yo with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever whose parents decline doxycycline over concerns about dental staining → Give doxycycline → a study found no staining of permanent teeth after short courses (5 to 10 days)
  5. 40 yo with summer tick exposure, fever, headache, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases, with no rash → Ehrlichiosis → doxycycline treats it as well
  6. The mechanism of thrombocytopenia in Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Intravascular platelet destruction from infection of vascular endothelium → small-vessel vasculitis
  7. 12 yo with severe abdominal pain and fever, a maculopapular rash on the wrists and ankles, and a normal abdominal CT → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → abdominal pain in children mimics appendicitis
  8. Child already started on doxycycline for suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Rickettsia serology → confirmation is retrospective and never delays therapy
  9. 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of high fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area, often bitten by mosquitoes; finished a steroid course for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill; T 39 C; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → doxycycline now, without waiting for serology
  10. 10 yo F back 5 days from 2 weeks in the Dominican Republic; fever 39.5 °C, retro-orbital headache, severe bone and muscle pain; macular truncal rash; no outdoor exposure in the US; white blood cell count 2,800/µL, platelets 90,000/µL → Dengue fever → supportive care with fluids; avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
  11. 4 yo M on a Tennessee farm in July: 4 days of fever and headache; conjunctival injection; wrist and ankle macules, now petechial, spread to palms, soles and trunk; no cracked lips or hand swelling; platelets 85,000/µL, sodium 130 mEq/L → Start doxycycline → Rocky Mountain spotted fever; any age, treat on suspicion
Decoy note Two details suggest abdominal and hepatic causes. Worsening abdominal pain with a normal CT fits RMSF: its abdominal pain may mimic appendicitis and is frequent in children. Once the scan is negative, stop pursuing an abdominal cause. Confusion with transaminitis suggests Wilson disease, but confusion in RMSF is early encephalitis arriving over hours, not over months.
Decoy note: no tick in the stem No tick – most RMSF stems never mention one; the clue is season (late spring to summer), rural or outdoor life, days of fever and severe headache, then a rash that starts on the wrists, ankles, palms or soles and spreads inward, turning petechial · Mosquito bites – point to dengue only with tropical travel, and dengue brings retro-orbital pain and severe bone and muscle pain · Conjunctival injection – occurs in RMSF too; Kawasaki disease needs 5 days of fever plus its criteria, and measles needs cough, coryza and a rash from the hairline down · Steroids for poison ivy a month ago – irrelevant; they explain none of the fever, headache or petechiae
Pearls Treat on suspicion, confirm retrospectively – doxycycline treats the patient; serology only documents the diagnosis · Doxycycline is given to children of any age for RMSF – the staining concern applies to prolonged courses, and withholding it is the dangerous choice · Low platelets plus transaminitis plus hyponatremia after outdoor exposure – a rickettsial fingerprint the viral exanthems do not produce · The rash moves inward – extremity onset spreading centrally with palms and soles is a short differential: RMSF, secondary syphilis, coxsackie hand-foot-and-mouth · No recalled tick bite – does not lower suspicion; the exposure history is habitat, not bite · Abdominal pain in a febrile child with a rash is part of the illness – a normal CT should redirect you to a systemic diagnosis, not a more invasive abdominal one
Pairs with Skin and Soft Tissue Infection covers the febrile-rash differential.
Fever and Rash in a Child covers measles and roseola.
Kawasaki Disease covers 5 days of fever with red eyes.
Ask: where did the rash start, and what did the platelets and transaminases do?
How NBME framed it Kawasaki disease appeared under its formal name, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, as a decoy for a child with 4 days of fever, red eyes and a petechial rash on the palms.
Transferable rule When the confirmatory test is retrospective and the untreated disease is lethal, treat on the clinical picture. Let the serology arrive whenever it arrives. A pending test is not a reason to wait; treatment should already have started.
Salient decoyStool for ova and parasites: fever with abdominal pain and liver enzymes fits amebiasis, but that causes bloody diarrhea and a liver abscess and explains no rash.
Treat-the-numberPrednisone: platelets of 46,000 invite ITP (immune thrombocytopenia), but ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child, not fever with rash, transaminitis and hypotension.
True-fact-wrong-slotAmoxicillin: correct for Lyme, same season and habitat, but Lyme rash is a single expanding annular lesion and it spares the platelets and liver.
Salient decoySerum ceruloplasmin: liver enzymes plus confusion reads as Wilson disease, a chronic disorder with Kayser-Fleischer rings, not four days of fever with a rash.
Sequencing trapLaparoscopy: the abdominal CT is already normal, which answers the surgical question.
Salient decoyDengue fever: mosquito bites suggest it, but without tropical travel dengue is not on the table. It brings retro-orbital and bone pain rather than a rash spreading in from the wrists.
Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: red eyes fit, but fever has run 4 days, not 5, and the rash is petechial on the palms, not polymorphous with swollen hands.
Salient decoyMeasles: conjunctivitis tempts, but measles rash starts at the hairline, spares the palms and soles, and follows cough and coryza.
